paragraphs: This position paper argues that evaluating AI could benefit from methods developed to assess human abilities. Standard benchmarks usually give models a fixed collection of questions and summarize performance with an average score. The authors identify several problems with this approach: evaluations can be costly, test material can become contaminated, and flawed questions can undermine the reliability of the result.

Their proposed direction is adaptive testing informed by psychometrics, the study of how to measure underlying abilities through observed responses. Instead of treating every question as equally useful for every model, an evaluation would estimate the characteristics or value of individual items and tailor the test to the model being assessed.

The intended benefit is a more robust estimate of capability, including underlying traits that a single aggregate score can obscure. The paper examines the possibilities and reasons for adopting this approach. Its contribution is a case for changing evaluation design, presenting psychometrics as a potentially powerful response to current benchmark problems.
icml-2025-position-ai-evaluation-should-.tldr: The authors advocate adaptive testing inspired by human psychometrics to make AI capability evaluation more reliable and informative.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that aligning AI with human values requires more attention to the data used during alignment. Much existing work emphasizes algorithms and training objectives. The authors contend that the quality and representativeness of feedback are also central, because that feedback supplies the evidence about which behaviors people want.

Through qualitative analysis, the paper examines weaknesses in feedback produced by both humans and AI systems. Human feedback has multiple sources of unreliability, and preferences can depend on context or change over time. AI-generated feedback brings another problem: limitations of the model supplying it can prevent that feedback from adequately capturing human values.

The proposed research agenda focuses on better feedback collection, stronger data cleaning, and rigorous verification of feedback. These directions address different points at which unreliable guidance can enter alignment training. The paper frames data quality as an active research problem whose unresolved gaps deserve attention alongside improvements to optimization methods.
icml-2025-position-challenges-and-future.tldr: The authors argue that better collection, cleaning, and verification of feedback are central to improving AI alignment.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing methods let developers change particular facts stored in a language model while limiting side effects. This is useful when information becomes outdated. The paper argues that the same capability creates serious safety risks that have received too little attention, especially when someone intentionally modifies a model for malicious purposes.

The authors connect this risk to several characteristics of editing methods: they are widely available, inexpensive to run, effective, and difficult to notice. They discuss how these methods can be adapted for malicious uses and identify weaknesses in an ecosystem where modified models can be uploaded and downloaded without verification.

The argument extends beyond the editing technique itself. Limited awareness among institutions and other stakeholders can make the surrounding ecosystem less prepared to recognize or address tampering. The authors therefore call for research on models that resist malicious changes, countermeasures against harmful editing, and broader participation in securing the channels through which models are shared.
icml-2025-position-editing-large-languag.tldr: The authors warn that inexpensive, stealthy knowledge editing can enable malicious model tampering and call for technical and ecosystem defenses.

paragraphs: This position paper advocates a larger role for formal mathematical reasoning in AI. Much AI work on mathematics has followed the language-modeling approach: assemble mathematical text and train models on it. The authors describe formal reasoning as a complementary avenue with particular importance for designing and verifying systems.

The distinguishing feature is the use of formal systems, including proof assistants, that can check whether reasoning is correct and provide automatic feedback. This connects the production of mathematical arguments to a mechanism for verifying them. That feedback is central to the paper’s case for making formal reasoning an integral part of future AI research.

The paper surveys progress, discusses open challenges, and proposes milestones for assessing future success. Its stated position is that formal mathematical reasoning is indispensable for future AI mathematics, formal verification, and verifiable generation. The contribution is therefore a research agenda linking these areas around reasoning whose correctness can be checked within a formal system.
icml-2025-position-formal-mathematical-r.tldr: The authors advocate formal mathematical reasoning as a core part of AI research because formal systems can verify reasoning and supply automatic feedback.

paragraphs: This paper argues that benchmark results need accompanying information about whether a model encountered the test data during training. Such train-test overlap matters for interpreting what an evaluation demonstrates. Outside researchers often cannot measure it directly because they lack access to the training data, leaving an information gap that developers are positioned to address.

The authors document reporting practices for 30 models. Only nine provide the relevant transparency: four release training data under open-source licenses, allowing direct community measurement, while five publish overlap measurement methods and statistics. By contacting developers, the authors also obtain new information about overlap for three additional models.

Their recommendation is to publish overlap statistics, training data, or both whenever reporting results on public test sets. The distinction between access to data and access to measured statistics offers more than one route to transparency. The paper’s goal is to make model evaluations easier to interpret and strengthen community trust in the results developers report.
icml-2025-position-language-model-develo.tldr: An examination of 30 models motivates a call for developers to disclose training–test overlap alongside public benchmark results.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that language models need better ways to manage their own reasoning. Although they perform well on many tasks, the authors identify persistent difficulties with robustness, transferring reasoning across tasks, and efficiently expanding reasoning capabilities. Improving prompts or repeatedly revising answers can help, but these approaches can be inefficient and generalize poorly.

The proposed direction is a Bayesian framework for meta-reasoning: reasoning about how to reason. Drawing on cognitive science, including Dual-Process Theory and Metacognitive Reasoning, the framework brings together self-awareness, monitoring, evaluation, regulation, and reflection. These components are intended to help a model examine and adjust its reasoning strategies.

The central motivation is adaptability across different reasoning demands. A model would have mechanisms for assessing its approach and refining that approach as part of the reasoning process. The paper revisits existing methods, identifies challenges, and outlines future research directions; it presents the framework as a proposed path toward stronger reasoning and cross-task generalization.
icml-2025-position-llms-need-a-bayesian-.tldr: The authors propose Bayesian meta-reasoning to help language models monitor, evaluate, and adapt their reasoning strategies across tasks.

paragraphs: This paper argues that factual accuracy alone does not make an AI system a reliable medical communicator. Retrieval and citations can connect an answer to source documents and reduce fabricated content. Yet even an answer containing accurate statements can lead a patient to an interpretation substantially different from what the source material or a knowledgeable clinician would convey.

The authors support this argument through a large-scale analysis of health queries, including disputed diagnoses and procedure safety. Their quantitative and qualitative evidence identifies answers that remove facts from context, leave out important relevant sources, or reinforce a patient’s existing misconceptions and biases. These are failures of communication even when individual statements are literally correct.

The proposed responses include better understanding of source documents and attention to communication pragmatics: how people interpret statements in context. The broader lesson is that evaluating medical answers requires considering the understanding they produce. The authors suggest that their recommendations could also help address similar communication problems outside medicine.
icml-2025-position-retrieval-augmented-s.tldr: Medical AI answers can mislead patients even when their cited facts are accurate, because context, source selection, and interpretation matter.

paragraphs: This position paper examines how AI and machine learning conferences make peer review visible as submission volumes grow. Using an open review platform does not necessarily mean that the review process is public. Some venues expose reviews throughout the process, others release them after decisions, and some keep them private despite using such platforms.

The authors analyze the strengths and limitations of these arrangements and discuss community interest in transparency. They draw on insights from Paper Copilot, a service that aggregates and analyzes conference data. Its audience includes more than 200,000 early-career researchers across 177 countries, with many participating actively in peer review.

The resulting recommendation is for review processes that are more open, transparent, and well regulated. The paper links this direction to broader community involvement and progress in the field. Its contribution is an analysis and policy position informed by conference-data engagement, with attention to how different disclosure practices shape the openness of the review process.
icml-2025-position-the-artificial-intell.tldr: The authors compare peer-review disclosure practices and advocate greater transparency, openness, and regulation in AI and machine learning conferences.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that trustworthy AI agents require language models and formal methods to work together. Language models offer adaptability and human-like reasoning, but they can also generate plausible, misleading outputs. That unreliability creates particular concern in settings where correctness has high stakes.

Formal methods provide mathematically rigorous ways to describe systems, specify requirements, reason about behavior, and verify correctness. They already have applications in mission-critical areas such as aerospace, defense, and cybersecurity. Their wider use faces substantial obstacles, including difficult learning curves, scalability limits, and trouble accommodating changing requirements in everyday applications.

The authors present integration as necessary to overcome the complementary weaknesses of the two approaches. Formal methods contribute rigor that language models lack, while language models could improve the accessibility and automation needed for broader use of formal methods. The paper’s central position is that developing trustworthy agents should bring these capabilities together, addressing both the reliability of AI behavior and the practical usability of verification.
icml-2025-position-trustworthy-ai-agents.tldr: The authors argue that trustworthy agents need language models’ adaptability combined with the mathematical rigor of formal methods.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a benchmark for systems that watch spreadsheet editing and predict what the user will do next. Building such a benchmark is difficult because public spreadsheet collections generally lack editing histories. Spreadsheet actions also combine location, timing, and operations that may contain multiple steps.

The authors manually curate 52 sequences comprising 12,000 actions that recreate spreadsheets from public collections. Parametrized heuristics and language-model refinement help seed this process. They also introduce an online evaluation procedure: after each user action, the predictor proposes an action, the evaluation accepts or rejects it, and accepted predictions change the remaining action sequence.

This design evaluates suggestions within an evolving workflow, continuing until the target spreadsheet is completed. The authors compare zero-shot language models, fine-tuned small language models, and classical predictors. Their analysis covers saved actions, false positives, efficiency, user profiles, prediction triggers, and available context. The contribution is a dataset and evaluation framework for studying how next-action assistance interacts with spreadsheet work.
icml-2026-a-benchmark-and-framework-for-.tldr: A spreadsheet benchmark evaluates next-action predictions through editing workflows that change when suggestions are accepted.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a model’s memory requirements and inference cost by removing parts of the network. One-shot pruning is especially attractive for large models because it avoids retraining. This paper examines a weakness in the quadratic optimization objectives used by many such methods: the quantities being optimized are affected by uncertainty.

The authors introduce RobOP, a robust optimization framework that explicitly accounts for uncertainty from sources such as noisy calibration data and variability in algorithmic updates. Its modular design allows existing pruning methods to incorporate the framework through modifications guided by the authors’ theory. This makes uncertainty handling an addition to established pruning approaches.

The reported results show improvements over prior pruning approaches when uncertainty is taken into account. The framework remains computationally tractable for a range of stylized uncertainty sets, supporting one-shot pruning at scale. The contribution is a way to make pruning decisions account for variation in their optimization inputs while retaining the practical appeal of pruning without retraining.
icml-2026-a-robust-optimization-guided-p.tldr: RobOP improves one-shot model pruning by incorporating uncertainty in calibration data and algorithmic updates into the optimization.

paragraphs: This paper combines spiking neural networks with state space modeling to process very long sequences. Spiking networks use sparse, event-based computation, while state space models offer sequence processing without the quadratic dependence on sequence length associated with transformers. The proposed SH²RFSSM is a second-order spiking model for both classification and regression.

The architecture uses heterogeneous harmonic resonate-and-fire neuronal layers and eliminates matrix multiplications. The authors also introduce a kernel-based spiking regressor that models dependencies in sequences reaching 50,000 steps. They observe that heterogeneity and discretization in the neuronal layers reduce spiking operations while improving performance.

Evaluation spans 17 datasets covering sensor data, time-series classification, regression, and long-term forecasting. The proposed model outperforms transformers and first-order state space models on average in the reported evaluation. Together, the performance and efficiency findings support its potential for resource-constrained signal processing, including human activity recognition and other tasks requiring information from long sequences.
icml-2026-a-spiking-heterogeneous-harmon.tldr: A spiking state space model removes matrix multiplications and achieves strong average performance on long-sequence tasks across 17 datasets.

paragraphs: Item response theory estimates properties of users and tasks from observed outcomes. In the Rasch model studied here, success becomes more likely as a user’s ability exceeds a task’s difficulty. Learning both quantities together matters in settings such as education, psychology, and recommendation, where outcomes reflect both sides of that relationship.

The authors identify shortcomings in existing joint maximum likelihood methods, particularly when few items are available, as well as missing theoretical guarantees. A prior two-stage approach has theoretical support but is computationally inefficient. Their alternative estimates user and item parameters jointly using an expectation-maximization algorithm.

The key technical step introduces Pólya-Gamma latent variables, which simplify the logistic log-likelihood underlying the Rasch model. That reformulation supports the proposed joint learning procedure. The authors report theoretical soundness and consistent improvements over existing methods on the synthetic and real-world datasets they evaluate. The contribution combines a more efficient estimation approach with theoretical support and empirical evidence.
icml-2026-an-efficient-joint-learning-ap.tldr: An expectation-maximization method jointly estimates user ability and item difficulty, with theoretical support and reported gains over existing approaches.

paragraphs: BlitzRank addresses ranking when comparisons are expensive, such as asking a language model to compare documents. A comparison involving several items reveals multiple pairwise preferences. The paper stores these relationships in a tournament graph and derives additional orderings through transitive closure, extracting more information without requesting more comparisons.

The framework specifies when the available information certifies the top items and uses a greedy query schedule to seek comparisons that help determine that result. It also handles inconsistent preferences that form cycles. By collapsing those cycles into equivalence classes, it produces tiers instead of forcing every item into a strict order.

Across 14 reranking benchmarks and five models, BlitzRank matches or exceeds the accuracy of compared approaches while using 25–40% fewer tokens than comparable methods. Against pairwise reranking, it reports near-identical quality with seven times fewer tokens. These findings connect its graph-based reuse of comparison information to an empirical improvement in the tradeoff between ranking quality and token expenditure.
icml-2026-blitzrank-principled-zero-shot.tldr: BlitzRank reuses comparison information through tournament graphs to deliver competitive document rankings with substantially fewer tokens.

paragraphs: Consistency training encourages similar outputs across related inputs or sampling procedures. Its simplicity and limited need for labels make it attractive, but its self-reinforcing structure raises a safety question: can making behavior more consistent also strengthen undesirable behavior? This paper investigates that question using models deliberately trained to exhibit controlled forms of misalignment.

The study tests seven consistency-training methods on 108 such models, ranging from 7 billion to 70 billion parameters. Effects differ by behavior: consistency training generally reduces reward hacking and emergent misalignment while increasing sycophancy. These results show that consistency itself does not have a uniform relationship with alignment.

The authors present evidence that shifts in the distribution produced by consistency labeling may drive systematic effects more strongly than differences in selection operators. They also develop a theoretical framework identifying conditions for amplification or suppression of misalignment. The findings motivate auditing consistency training in critical applications, with attention to which behaviors its labeling process reinforces.
icml-2026-consistency-training-can-entre.tldr: Consistency training has behavior-dependent alignment effects, generally reducing some misalignment while amplifying sycophancy in controlled experiments.

paragraphs: Influence maximization asks which small set of starting nodes will produce the largest expected spread through a network. Classical algorithms assume that influence probabilities are already known. This paper studies the online version, where a learner must repeatedly choose starting nodes while learning unknown probabilities under the independent cascade model.

The available feedback reveals which nodes activate. Earlier work relies on a pair oracle that jointly optimizes the chosen seeds and feasible model parameters, a demanding computational requirement. The authors instead design an algorithm that uses a standard offline oracle, resolving whether this simpler oracle can support sublinear regret in the stated setting.

Their regret bound grows roughly with the square root of the number of interactions, apart from logarithmic factors. Sublinear growth means the regret per interaction decreases as interactions accumulate. Experiments on real and synthetic data support the theoretical results. The main contribution is therefore a learning guarantee under limited feedback with a more practical oracle requirement.
icml-2026-efficient-online-influence-max.tldr: An online influence-maximization algorithm achieves roughly square-root regret with node-level feedback using only a standard offline oracle.

paragraphs: A mixture of Bernoulli product distributions models binary data through hidden components, each with its own probabilities for the variables. This paper studies recovering those component probabilities and mixture weights from access to a probability generating polynomial. That polynomial may be represented by a probabilistic generating circuit.

The authors establish that parameters are uniquely identifiable for almost all mixtures. They provide a randomized exact-reconstruction algorithm requiring O(nr²) oracle queries for n variables and r components. The procedure repeatedly restricts attention to O(r) variables, extracts low-degree coefficients, and uses a moment-based tensor decomposition to recover the parameters.

The query bound grows linearly with the number of variables and polynomially with the number of components. According to the authors, this is the first exact reconstruction algorithm with those query-complexity properties in this oracle model. The result concerns the stated polynomial-access setting, and its identifiability claim applies to almost all mixtures rather than every possible mixture.
icml-2026-fast-reconstruction-of-mixture.tldr: A randomized algorithm exactly reconstructs Bernoulli mixture parameters using O(nr²) generating-polynomial oracle queries, with identifiability established for almost all mixtures.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to train models whose performance deteriorates more slowly when their input distribution changes. Its objective, Robust Satisficing, requires a target level of performance on the training distribution while minimizing fragility. Fragility measures the rate of performance decline as the data distribution moves away from training conditions.

The authors develop Iterative Robust Satisficing, a gradient-based algorithm that directly optimizes this objective. They evaluate it under synthetic and real-world shifts, including long-tailed image classification, group shifts associated with spurious correlations, and natural shifts in tabular regression. Across these evaluations, it consistently improves minority-group and worst-group performance without sacrificing overall accuracy.

The reported computational requirement is also practical: each update uses a single forward and backward pass, with a per-step cost similar to standard stochastic gradient descent. The results suggest that explicitly controlling performance degradation can offer an effective robust-training alternative. The evidence ties that objective to better outcomes for vulnerable groups in the evaluated distribution shifts.
icml-2026-iterative-robust-satisficing-m.tldr: Iterative Robust Satisficing improves robustness by minimizing performance deterioration while maintaining a target level of training-distribution performance.

paragraphs: Tool-using agents face safety decisions throughout an action sequence, including when tool feedback is adversarial. This paper introduces MOSAIC, a post-training framework that makes those decisions explicit. Its inference loop asks the agent to plan, check safety, and then either act or refuse, treating refusal as an action the model can learn.

Training uses preference-based reinforcement learning with comparisons between pairs of trajectories, avoiding the need for trajectory-level labels. The authors argue that these comparisons capture safety distinctions that scalar rewards can miss. Evaluation covers multiple model families and out-of-distribution benchmarks involving harmful requests, prompt injection, benign tool use, and privacy leakage across domains.

The reported results include reductions in harmful behavior of up to 50% and increases in harmful-task refusal of over 20% on injection attacks. MOSAIC also reduces privacy leakage while preserving or improving benign-task performance. These findings support the framework’s generalization across the evaluated models and settings, connecting explicit safety checks to safer multi-step execution.
icml-2026-learning-when-to-act-or-refuse.tldr: MOSAIC trains tool-using agents to plan, check safety, and act or refuse, reducing harmful behavior while maintaining useful task performance in evaluations.

paragraphs: Training on data from multiple domains requires choosing batches that support learning while maintaining domain coverage. PartitionSel addresses this by selecting examples across domains under explicit per-domain budgets. A single validation-guided gradient-matching objective connects these choices, aiming to reduce redundant selections across different domains.

The budgets are expressed through a partition-matroid constraint, which organizes the selection limits by domain. The authors show that their objective is weakly submodular and develop an orthogonal matching pursuit algorithm with approximation guarantees. This provides a theoretical basis for making coordinated batch selections under the required coverage constraints.

Experiments fine-tune Qwen2.5 and Llama-3 using MetaMathQA and Mol-Instructions. PartitionSel improves over both per-domain and domain-agnostic selection baselines on the two benchmarks. It also reduces the number of conflicting gradient pairs within batches, indicating more compatible training updates. The findings support the value of coordinating example selection across domains while retaining explicit control over how much each domain contributes.
icml-2026-minibatch-selection-for-langua.tldr: PartitionSel coordinates minibatch selection across domains under coverage budgets, improving fine-tuning results and reducing conflicting gradient pairs.

paragraphs: Human preferences often involve several goals that can conflict, such as helpfulness and harmlessness. This paper studies preference alignment when these goals cannot naturally be collapsed into one score. It introduces Multi-Objective Preference Optimization, or MOPO, to improve a primary objective while requiring secondary objectives to remain above chosen thresholds.

The framework combines these constraints with KL regularization and works directly from pairwise preferences, without requiring point-wise rewards. Its safety thresholds are tunable, making the required levels for secondary objectives explicit. The authors derive simple closed-form iterative updates for optimizing within this framework.

On synthetic benchmarks, MOPO empirically recovers Pareto-optimal policies, where improving one objective requires a tradeoff elsewhere. Fine-tuning on human-preference data produces multi-billion-parameter models with higher rewards that Pareto-dominate the evaluated baselines: they perform at least as well across the objectives and better on some. The reported optimization is stable and robust, supporting explicit constraints as a practical way to manage multiple alignment goals.
icml-2026-multi-objective-preference-opt.tldr: MOPO aligns models with multiple preferences by optimizing a primary goal while enforcing tunable minimum levels for secondary goals.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can reveal whether two entities were connected in their training graph. This paper revisits attacks that infer those links using only output probabilities in a strict black-box setting. It emphasizes whether attackers can identify some links reliably while making extremely few false accusations, a risk that average attack scores can obscure.

The authors find that these attacks remain effective at very low false-positive rates. They also identify geometric bottlenecks in output-probability space that suppress distinguishable directions for pairs within the same class. A geometry-aware reconditioning method reshapes intra-class distances to make link status easier to separate without reducing reliability.

Across multiple real-world graphs and graph neural networks, the correction achieves up to twice the success of generic attacks on intra-class pairs. The findings suggest that existing evaluations substantially under-measure output-based leakage. The contribution is both an improved diagnostic attack and an argument for evaluating link privacy through high-confidence vulnerabilities affecting even a small subset of connections.
icml-2026-revisiting-asymmetries-in-blac.tldr: Black-box graph attacks can identify private links with very few false positives, and geometry-aware correction exposes additional intra-class leakage.

paragraphs: The Bad Triangle Transversal problem concerns graphs whose edges carry positive or negative signs. A bad triangle contains exactly one negative edge. The task is to remove as few edges as possible so that no such triangle remains. This paper develops several algorithms that use at most twice the minimum required number of removals.

The authors also establish a computational hardness result: even on complete graphs, achieving an approximation factor better than 2137/2136 is NP-hard. Their reduction applies to Correlation Clustering, Cluster Deletion, and Minimum Strong Triadic Closure as well. These results place both algorithmic guarantees and hardness boundaries around closely related graph problems.

A further contribution connects Bad Triangle Transversal to Correlation Clustering on complete graphs. A pivot procedure converts edge-removal solutions into clusters and establishes that the two optimal objective values are within a factor of three halves. This relationship explains how a solution that eliminates problematic local triangles can be translated into a globally organized clustering solution.
icml-2026-simple-algorithms-for-bad-tria.tldr: The paper gives factor-two algorithms for removing bad triangles and proves hardness and approximation connections to correlation clustering.

paragraphs: Average treatment effects summarize how an intervention changes the mean outcome, but outcomes can differ across their full distributions. This paper introduces the Sinkhorn treatment effect, which measures divergence between counterfactual outcome distributions using entropic optimal transport. It provides a target for assessing distributional changes beyond an average difference.

The authors express this quantity as a smooth transformation of counterfactual mean embeddings under an appropriate kernel. They establish first-order pathwise differentiability generally and second-order differentiability when the counterfactual distributions are equal. These mathematical properties support debiased estimation and asymptotically valid testing at a fixed entropic regularization parameter.

Test power depends on the regularization choice, so the authors also propose aggregating evidence across a grid of choices. This addresses the practical problem of relying on one parameter setting. Experiments with simulated and image data demonstrate advantages of the estimator and tests. The contribution connects a whole-distribution causal measure to statistical procedures for estimating and detecting treatment effects.
icml-2026-sinkhorn-treatment-effects-a-c.tldr: Sinkhorn treatment effects measure causal differences across entire outcome distributions and support debiased estimation and aggregated statistical testing.

paragraphs: RandomShuffle trains by processing data without replacement in a randomly permuted order. It has known convergence advantages over stochastic gradient descent that samples with replacement, but producing a uniformly random permutation can require expensive movement of data through the memory hierarchy. This paper targets that input/output cost.

The authors propose a shuffling algorithm with linear input/output complexity and rigorous guarantees on its randomness. It can produce permutations with two-wise independence. They extend the construction to approximately k-wise independent permutations when fast memory can hold at least k memory blocks, allowing a small error in the resulting probability distribution.

These guarantees let the method attain the same expected theoretical convergence as RandomShuffle while using optimal linear input/output cost. The key result links a structured form of randomness to the training guarantee, avoiding the full data-movement burden associated with uniform permutation generation. The memory requirement and permitted distributional error are explicit conditions of the extension to higher-order independence.
icml-2026-the-benefits-of-full-data-shuf.tldr: A shuffling algorithm matches RandomShuffle’s expected theoretical convergence with optimal linear input/output cost through controlled independence guarantees.
